long_biography.plain_text:
Aramex found its niche by acting as the Middle Eastern delivery partner for international couriers that lacked their own regional networks. Fadi Ghandour built the company around an asset-light wholesale model, using local agents while adopting the technology and operating standards of larger partners. This let a small Amman start-up compete without buying aircraft or extensive warehouse infrastructure.

Ghandour also shaped Aramex through decentralised decision-making. He recruited young regional graduates alongside experienced freight specialists, then encouraged staff to pursue opportunities without waiting for central approval. Aramex became the first Arab-world company listed on Nasdaq in 1997. Ghandour eventually handed executive leadership to an internally developed successor, ending three decades as chief executive while preserving the organisation's entrepreneurial culture.
